```{r libs}
library(agetime)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
```

This vignette describes errors and difficulties you might
encounter when using `agetime`, and suggests solutions.


# Reading labels

## "Don't know how to interpret label"

### Problem

A label is in a format that `agetime` does not recognize.

```{r unparsed-problem, error = TRUE}
x <- c("0-4", "5-9", "Everything", "85+ (a)")
age_standard(x)
```

### Solution

The error message lists the labels that cannot be interpreted. Clean
these labels before passing them to `agetime`.

```{r unparsed-clean}
x_clean <- x
x_clean[x_clean == "Everything"] <- "Total"
x_clean[x_clean == "85+ (a)"] <- "85+"
age_standard(x_clean)
```

### Discussion

`agetime` recognizes many common formats, including:

- ranges such as `"5-9"`, `"5 to 9"`, `"5--9"`, and `"5-9 years"`;
- open age groups such as `"85+"`, `"85 and over"`, `"85 or more"`,
  `"85 years and older"`, and `"85 & over"`;
- age groups starting at 0, such as `"Under 5"`, `"less than 5"`, `"<5"`,
  and `"Infant"`;
- ages from 0 up to and including a stated age, such as `"5 or younger"`
  and `"5 and younger"`, which become `"0-5"`;
- totals such as `"Total"` and `"All ages"`, and
- missing values such as `"Not stated"`, `"Unknown"`, and `"Age not stated"`.

Case, spaces, and leading zeros are ignored.


## One-year periods written as ranges

### Problem

A period label such as `"2020-2021"` gives an error.

```{r one-year-problem, error = TRUE}
period_standard("2020-2021")
```

### Solution

By default, period and cohort functions read `"2020-2021"` as the
interval from the start of 2020 to the start of 2021, which is a single
year. `agetime` expects single years to be written as `"2020"`.
If `"2020-2021"` denotes the two-year period consisting of
the years 2020 and 2021, then set `interpret_multi`
to `"below_upper"`.

```{r one-year-solution}
period_standard("2020-2021", interpret_multi = "below_upper")
```

### See Also

- The section on rules for interpreting inputs in `?period_lower`


## Financial and academic years: "Lower limit greater than upper limit"

### Problem

Financial and academic years that start part way
through the calendar year are sometimes described
using labels such as `"2019/20"` or `"2019-20"`.
`agetime` currently does not know how to interpret these
labels. For instance, it interprets `"2019/20"`
as describing a period that starts in the year 2019
and ends in the year 20.

```{r fiscal-problem, error = TRUE}
period_standard("2019/20")
```

### Solution

Calculate the end year and pass it to `agetime`
with `interpret_single` set to `"upper"`.

```{r fiscal-solution}
fy <- c("2019/20", "2020-21", "1999/00")
fy_end <- as.integer(substr(fy, 1L, 4L)) + 1
fy_end
period_interval(fy_end, interpret_single = "upper")
period_mid(fy_end, interpret_single = "upper")
```

The same approach works for cohorts.

### See Also

- The section on rules for interpreting inputs in `?period_lower`
  and `?cohort_lower`


## Single-year periods that appear to overlap with open intervals

### Problem

When the labels for single-year periods are based on the upper limits
of the periods, the labels can appear to overlap with open intervals.
In the series `"2019", "2020", "2020+"`, for instance, the label `"2020"`
appears to overlap with the label `"2020+"`.

### Solution

Although they look strange, series such as `"2019", "2020", "2020+"`
are in fact valid, if they use the upper-limit convention.
To see what is going on, use `period_interval()`.

```{r noncalendar-intervals}
period_interval(c("2019", "2020", "2020+"), interpret_single = "upper")
```

The `"2020"` label might refer, for instance, to the period
that starts at midnight on 1 July 2019 and ends at midnight on 1 July 2020,
while the `"2020+"` label refers to the period that starts
at midnight on 1 July 2020.

### Discussion

Series that use the upper-limit labelling convention and that
have open periods or cohorts are rare.

### See Also

- [Financial and academic years](#financial-and-academic-years-lower-limit-greater-than-upper-limit)
- `period_interval()` and `cohort_interval()`
- The section on rules for interpreting inputs in `?period_lower`
  and `?cohort_lower`


# Checking labels

## Different labels for the same age group

### Problem

`age_assert_values()` or `age_diagnose_values()` reports an overlap,
even though the age groups look distinct.

```{r synonyms-problem, error = TRUE}
x <- c("0", "infant", "1-4", "5+")
age_assert_values(x, no_overlap = TRUE)
```

### Solution

Two different labels, `"0"` and `"infant"`, describe the same age group.
Standardizing the labels makes this visible.

```{r synonyms-solution}
age_standard(x)
```

You will then need to decide what to do about the repeated
values. See [Overlaps in a data frame with repeated age
groups](#overlap-df) for one possible approach.


## Overlaps in a data frame with repeated age groups {#overlap-df}

### Problem

`age_assert_values()` reports an overlap in a column of a data frame
where each age group appears once for each sex, region, or year.

```{r repeats-problem, error = TRUE}
df <- tibble(
  age = c("0-4", "5-9", "0-4", "5-9"),
  sex = c("F", "F", "M", "M")
)
df |>
  mutate(age = age_assert_values(age, no_overlap = TRUE))
```

### Solution

Check within groups.

```{r repeats-solution}
df |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  mutate(age = age_assert_values(age, no_overlap = TRUE))
```

### See Also

- Cookbook: [Check labels within groups of a data frame](cookbook.html#validate-labels-groups)


## Totals and missing values

### Problem

A check fails, or a function such as `age_extend()` or
`age_coarsen_to()` gives an error, because the labels include a total
or a missing value.

```{r totals-problem, error = TRUE}
x <- c("0-4", "5-9", "Total")
age_assert_values(x, no_total = TRUE)
```

### Solution

Use `age_is_total()` and `age_is_missing()` to find the
labels for totals or missing values. If appropriate,
remove the associated rows.

```{r totals-solution}
df <- tibble(
  age = c("0-4", "5-9", "Total", "Not stated"),
  count = c(10, 20, 35, 5)
)

df |>
  filter(!age_is_total(age), !age_is_missing(age))
```

### Discussion

`age_coarsen()`, `age_coarsen_five()`, and similar functions keep
totals and missing values as separate categories, so they do not need
to be removed first.

### See Also

- Cookbook: [Drop totals from a dataset](cookbook.html#drop-totals) and
  [Drop "Not stated" categories from a dataset](cookbook.html#drop-missing)


# Transforming labels

## Coarsening fails

### Problem

`age_coarsen()`, `age_coarsen_to()`, or one of their variants gives an
error.

```{r coarsen-problem, error = TRUE}
x <- c("0-4", "5-9", "12")
age_coarsen(x, breaks = c(0, 7, 10))
```

### Solution

The error message distinguishes two problems:

- A label *would be split* when it overlaps two or more new age groups.
  In the case above, `"5-9"` overlaps `"0-6"` and `"7-9"`.
  When a label would be split, move the breaks so that they
  fall between the old age groups.
- A label is *not fully covered* when it lies partly or wholly outside the
  new age groups. In the case above, `"12"` lies above 10.
  When a label is not fully covered, add breaks, or, for
  `age_coarsen()`, set `open_right = TRUE`.

```{r coarsen-solution}
age_coarsen(x, breaks = c(0, 10), open_right = TRUE)
```

With `age_coarsen_to()`, every label must lie inside one of the labels in
`to`. Add labels to `to`, or remove labels that should not be included.


## Unused levels disappear from tables

### Problem

You used a `fill` function to add age, period, or cohort
levels, but tidyverse functions `count()` or `summarise()`
drop these levels if they have no observations.

```{r unused-problem}
df <- tibble(
  age = c("0-4", "10-14", "0-4"),
  respondents = c(10, 20, 5)
) |>
  mutate(age = age_fill(age))

levels(df$age)

df |>
  count(age)
```

### Solution

Tidyverse functions drop unused factor levels by default. Use
`.drop = FALSE` to retain the unused levels.

```{r unused-solution}
df |>
  count(age, .drop = FALSE)

df |>
  group_by(age, .drop = FALSE) |>
  summarise(respondents = sum(respondents))
```

### See Also

- Cookbook: [Include levels that don't appear in the data](cookbook.html#fill-levels)


## Results are factors, not character vectors

### Problem

`age_coarsen()`, `age_fill()`, `age_set_open_right()`, and `age_set_order()`
return factors. They do this because factor levels can contain
useful information, such as labels that do not appear in the data.
But sometimes the task calls for a character vector, not a factor.

```{r factors-problem}
x <- c("0", "1-4", "5-9")
x |>
  age_coarsen_five()
```

### Solution

Call `as.character()` on the result.

```{r factors-solution}
x |>
  age_coarsen_five() |>
  as.character()
```


## Midpoints of open age groups

### Problem

`age_mid()` gives an error for an open age group within a grouped
calculation.

```{r mid-problem, error = TRUE}
df <- tibble(
  sex = c("F", "F", "M"),
  age = c("80-84", "85+", "85+")
)

df |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  mutate(mid = age_mid(age))
```

### Solution

`age_mid()` gives an open age group a midpoint based on the width of the
nearest closed age group. In the group `sex = "M"`, there is no closed age
group. Calculate midpoints before grouping.

```{r mid-solution}
df |>
  mutate(mid = age_mid(age))
```
